strengths: Addresses timely problem of whether RL post-training transcends base model support with clear theoretical framework
Introduces Likelihood Quantile (LQ) as natural and useful characterization of base model properties governing post-training complexity
Establishes minimax lower bounds (Theorems 10-12) proving the base model barrier is fundamental, not an artifact of the analysis
Process reward analysis elegantly shows token-level LQ avoids exponential dependence on sequence length N, providing valuable algorithmic alternative
High technical quality with sophisticated proof techniques: online-to-batch conversion, careful log-likelihood analysis, hard instance construction
Comprehensive coverage including outcome/process rewards, on/off-policy variants, constant/adaptive learning rates, establishing both upper and lower bounds
Adaptive learning rate analysis for SGD removing N dependence in Proposition 1 is non-trivial contribution
Clear logical progression from conditional convergence to LQ-based unconditional guarantees
weaknesses: Severely restricted to linear models with frozen feature maps far removed from practice; unclear how insights transfer to neural networks
Minimal experimental validation: only synthetic data satisfying Assumption 1 exactly; no realistic tasks or ablation studies; experiments merely confirm theory without new insights
Limited algorithmic contributions: analyzes basic REINFORCE rather than practical algorithms (PPO, GRPO) that motivated work; Algorithms 1-2 are somewhat artificial
Process reward assumptions quite strong: requires oracle access to r*(x, y₁:ᵢ) for all prefixes, while learning such reward models is acknowledged as hard problem left to future work
Significant gap between theory and practice: initialization at w₀=0 unsatisfying when practice uses pre-trained weights; frozen features contradict typical fine-tuning; only final layer trained
Likelihood Quantile concept lacks practical utility: unclear how to estimate Q_q(ε) from data; lower bound Q_q(ε)≤k^{-N}/(1-O(γ²nε)) is opaque; connection to existing coverage definitions unclear
Strong margin assumption (Assumption 1) only validated on synthetic data; unclear how real models satisfy token-level separability or how results degrade under violations

Technical presentation could be clearer: Q_q(ε)^{-1} vs Q^{-1}_q notation requires careful reading; relationship between conditional and unconditional bounds should be explained upfront; heavy O˜ notation hides factors
Fully on-policy PG variant (Proposition 20) has suboptimal rate and deferred to appendix, suggesting practical variant not well understood
No code provided; theoretical results lack implementable certificates; reproducibility limited to synthetic experiments

strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing practical observations about RL post-training limitations; clear connection to empirical findings that RL often just sharpens base distributions
Novel Likelihood Quantile (LQ) framework provides interpretable characterization of when post-training can extend beyond base model support
Comprehensive theoretical analysis with matching upper and lower bounds establishing minimax optimality; efficient online learning algorithm achieving O(k^N/γ²) mistake bound
Process rewards with token-level LQ offers concrete algorithmic solution achieving O(Nk+ε^{-1})/γ² queries vs exponential dependence for outcome rewards
Sound technical execution including adaptive learning rate analysis removing N from rates; clean reduction to online convex optimization
Empirical validation of key theoretical predictions (Figure 1: off-support plateau with ORM but improvement with PRM) and demonstration of base model barrier on real data
weaknesses: Highly restrictive model class (linear autoregressive, frozen features, single correct answer, binary rewards) bears limited resemblance to practical deep learning, limiting relevance of theoretical insights to real LLMs
Exponential dependence on sequence length N persists even with process rewards (O(Nk) term); for realistic settings (N≈100, k≈50k) this remains impractical

Base model barrier theorem (Theorem 12) shows unless supervised pre-training already achieves error ε, no algorithm can improve—fundamental negative result with limited algorithmic resolution despite PRM proposal
Large theory-practice gap: experiments only on synthetic data (N=128, k=32) and single real benchmark (Math500); no experiments on tasks with multiple valid solutions or noisy rewards
Assumption 1 (margin at token-level given correct history) is strong; paper provides no empirical verification on real tasks or guidance on when this holds
Limited algorithmic novelty—proofs build on standard online convex optimization and prior margin-based analyses ([Sha21, RSSW24]); main contribution is problem-specific rather than new techniques

Critical implementation details unclear: how to apply conditioning on unknown sample likelihood E_α at test time; computational cost of Algorithm 2's multiple reward queries per token; adaptive LR gradient norm computation overhead

Experimental validation insufficient: only ~500 Math problems with no error bars; synthetic scale modest; arbitrary thresholds (10^{-12} likelihood); no comparison to baselines like best-of-k sampling or ablation studies

strengths: Novel identification and theoretical characterization of the base model barrier—showing that policy gradient methods require exponentially many reward queries to go beyond base model support. This formalizes important empirical observations about LLM post-training limitations.

Rigorous and comprehensive theoretical analysis with matching upper bounds (Theorems 2-6) and matching lower bounds (Theorems 10-12), establishing near-minimax optimality. This provides a fairly complete picture of the problem landscape.

Introduction of Likelihood Quantile (LQ) as an elegant abstraction that captures base model quality and governs improvement potential. Token-level LQ for process rewards is a natural and useful refinement.

Solid technical contributions including adaptive learning rate analysis that removes sequence length dependence, minimax optimal algorithm for online autoregressive learning, and clear distinction between on-support and off-support complexity regimes.

Well-motivated problem formulation addressing practical questions about whether RL can create genuinely new knowledge beyond base model support, supported by empirical observations from real LLM post-training.

Comprehensive treatment covering outcome rewards, process rewards, conditional/unconditional convergence, online/statistical settings, with honest discussion of limitations and strong presentation overall.
weaknesses: Significant gap between theoretical model (linear autoregressive with frozen features) and practical systems (non-linear Transformers). Unclear how insights transfer to realistic settings, limiting practical applicability.

Restrictive and strong assumptions: (1) token-level margin condition is quite demanding, (2) Assumption 2 for process rewards is very specific, (3) access to perfect process rewards is unrealistic. While acknowledged, these substantially limit scope.

Weak experimental validation: synthetic experiments are small-scale (N=128, d=k=32); Qwen3 experiments only show LQ curves without validating convergence rates or comparing algorithmic performance. No experiments demonstrate theoretical predictions.
Incomplete reproducibility information: the line 'The results can be reproduced using .' contains a blank URL, and no code is provided. Experimental details could be more complete.

Limited analysis of process reward model learning. Section 4 assumes access to accurate process rewards but provides no guidance on obtaining them or analysis of robustness to reward model errors, acknowledged only as future work.

Very dense presentation (39 pages with appendix) that makes it challenging to extract key insights. Main introduction could better distill the novel contributions. Heavy notation (Õ, multiple quantile variants) adds complexity.
